OpenRouter is officially part of @stripe today!
More than 10 million developers and companies use OpenRouter, and as they build with more models across more workloads, they need control over what it costs and where their data goes.
OpenRouter has built that operating infrastructure to help run AI across every model and provider, with access to new models, uptime through outages, and enforced spend and data policies for each team.
Joining Stripe, which has spent years running critical infrastructure for businesses around the world, means we can build it faster and support companies at every scale.
Our commitment to neutrality stays the same. Models and providers compete on quality, reliability, and price. You decide what works for your business.
Stripe (@stripe)
OpenRouter is now part of Stripe.
Stripe is building the economic infrastructure for AI. Together with OpenRouter, we’ll help businesses explore new models and optimize token routing and usage.

Providers’ data-handling claims have mostly relied on self-attestation. This isn't going to be sufficient.
Just as continuous benchmarking and monitoring transformed the quality and reliability of inference both on and out of OpenRouter, we expect technical validation, auditing, and continuous testing to do the same for data policy enforcement.
Encrypted TEE (Trusted Execution Environment) inference will be a great way for providers to accelerate this.
We will keep raising the bar, and providers that want to be on OpenRouter will need to meet it.
OpenRouter (@OpenRouter)
Security researchers recently found data-handling problems with some inference providers available on OpenRouter. The findings showed no breach of OpenRouter itself.
In response, we’ve off-boarded 3 providers, removed many endpoints from ZDR eligibility, and notified affected customers.
We’re now building the researchers’ testing into ongoing checks. Full update and provider write-ups on our blog:
— https://x.com/OpenRouter/status/2124315081899200715
items.title_ja:
プロバイダーのデータ処理に関する主張は、ほとんどが自己証明に依存しています。これでは十分ではありません。
継続的なベンチマークとモニタリングによって OpenRouter 内外の推論の品質と信頼性が変化したのと同様に、データ ポリシーの適用に関しても技術的な検証、監査、継続的なテストが同様の効果をもたらすことを期待しています。
暗号化された TEE (信頼された実行環境) 推論は、プロバイダーにとってこれを加速する優れた方法になります。
私たちは基準を引き上げ続け、OpenRouter への参加を希望するプロバイダーはその基準を満たす必要があります。
オープンルーター (@OpenRouter)
セキュリティ研究者は最近、OpenRouter で利用できる一部の推論プロバイダーでデータ処理の問題を発見しました。調査結果では、OpenRouter 自体の侵害は認められませんでした。
これに応じて、私たちは 3 つのプロバイダーをオフボードし、多くのエンドポイントを ZDR 資格から削除し、影響を受ける顧客に通知しました。
私たちは現在、研究者によるテストを継続的なチェックに組み込んでいます。完全なアップデートとプロバイダーの記事はブログにあります。
— https://x.com/OpenRouter/status/2124315081899200715

The intensity with which the campaign against Jensen Huang continues unabated is almost absurd.
I couldn't find a single article that says anything even remotely good about Jensen.
A tragedy. All articles below are from *today*
Chubby♨️ (@kimmonismus)
Right now, the media is full of stories that paint Jensen Huang in a bad light. I have actually met Jensen, and I want to tell you a story. (1/2)
My interview with Jensen hasn't been published yet, which is probably understandable given the current situation. More on that when the time is right. But I had the chance to meet Jensen Huang in person several times while traveling through Europe with NVIDIA, and I want to tell you about it, especially about one experience that has stayed with me.
Some quick background: NVIDIA invited me to join Jensen's European tour last month, together with Bloomberg and Steve Nouri. We were there for every stop: Paris, London, Stockholm, Berlin. I was on site for every one of his public speeches.
A lot is being said right now about Jensen making statements that many find contemptible, while others take them with humor. And to be fair, Jensen does have a slightly edgy humor that rubs some people the wrong way. He speaks plainly, says what he thinks and makes jokes that can offend, but he always makes fun of himself too.
And I, at least, can say one thing very clearly: never once did I feel that any of his remarks were meant as an attack, as belittling or as humiliating. It was always situational comedy. If Jensen hadn't been CEO of NVIDIA, he would have made an outstanding stand-up comedian, always ready with a quip. But as we all know, that's a matter of taste, and saying that I always found it amusing won't calm anyone down.
So here are two stories that show Jensen really has a good heart, and that the campaign against him distorts his image.
This is my personal experience:
NVIDIA gave me the opportunity to do a 30-minute interview with Jensen in Stockholm.
As you can imagine, I was incredibly nervous. Honestly, I was even scared. Me, a small "content creator," getting to meet Jensen in person and talk to him. He makes time even for little people like me. I met him and his staff at a café in Stockholm. We went inside and, as was bound to happen, my camera gear fell out of my backpack onto the floor. My stress level: through the roof. But Jensen stayed calm and relaxed, told me everything was fine and that I didn't need to stress, and put his hand on my shoulder. Not one snide word, no making fun of me. Quite the opposite. He knew I was genuinely stressed and helped me relax.
Then we started the interview. And while we were talking, people kept coming into the café where we were recording. It was a café open to the public. And as you'd expect, the same thing happened again and again: while Jensen and I were talking, guests recognized him and more or less burst into our interview. And Jensen took time for every single one of them. Not one bad word, no irritation, no stupid remark. He gave every guest his time, took photos, had conversations. In the middle of the interview. I was surprised and genuinely moved. No arrogance on his part, just friendly humanity. And that's how an interview scheduled for 30 minutes turned into 60. Simply because Jensen and I had such a good conversation and he kindly gave all those guests extra time on top.
But the most impressive part actually came afterwards. We had been eating a Swedish pastry, it's called “fika” (at least that’s how we called it). And Jensen loved it. After we wrapped up the interview, Jensen went to the trunk of his car, grabbed some cash, went back into the café and bought “fika” for everyone. For himself, his security, his staff, for everyone.
No camera recorded it. Nothing done purely for PR. Nothing meant to make him "look better." Just a human gesture, because he liked the pastry and wanted everyone to enjoy it too. If I hadn't told this story today, it would never have been told. And to me it shows that Jensen is a genuinely good person.
I gain nothing from writing this. Jensen is no longer CEO. And nobody suggested I write this story down.

We're seeing major breakthroughs right now, like the proof of the quasi-Riemann hypothesis. What worries me is that the mood is turning, and that we might stop seeing breakthroughs like this.
Sentiment against AI keeps growing, especially against the data center buildout, and since the midterms data centers have become a political issue.
I'm not taking sides here. But everyone should be clear about what calling for a slowdown in the buildout actually means:
- Breakthroughs come slower
- Research into diseases and new therapies takes longer
- Competitors like China pull ahead
Yes, the concerns deserve to be taken seriously. But in a lot of recurring debates, the fear of superintelligence has lost touch with the facts and turned into plain resentment.
We need more debate on the merits, less fear, and above all an honest look at what we give up when we slow the buildout down.

- 病気や新しい治療法の研究には時間がかかる
- 中国などの競争相手が先を行く
はい、その懸念は真剣に受け止められるべきです。しかし、度重なる多くの議論の中で、超知性に対する恐怖は事実との乖離を失い、単純な憤りに変わってしまった。
私たちはメリットについてもっと議論し、恐怖を減らし、そして何よりも、建設を遅らせるときに何を放棄するのかについて正直に考える必要があります。

I never met Jensen but every single NVIDIA employee I’ve met, has told me a story of how he supported them personally, IE: helping them if they had long-term or serious illness, or remembering certain challenges facing their respective families.
These were told unprompted. Guess there is a reason why he has a 99% approval rating by NVIDIA employees on Glassdoor.
Chubby♨️ (@kimmonismus)
Right now, the media is full of stories that paint Jensen Huang in a bad light. I have actually met Jensen, and I want to tell you a story. (1/2)
My interview with Jensen hasn't been published yet, which is probably understandable given the current situation. More on that when the time is right. But I had the chance to meet Jensen Huang in person several times while traveling through Europe with NVIDIA, and I want to tell you about it, especially about one experience that has stayed with me.
Some quick background: NVIDIA invited me to join Jensen's European tour last month, together with Bloomberg and Steve Nouri. We were there for every stop: Paris, London, Stockholm, Berlin. I was on site for every one of his public speeches.
A lot is being said right now about Jensen making statements that many find contemptible, while others take them with humor. And to be fair, Jensen does have a slightly edgy humor that rubs some people the wrong way. He speaks plainly, says what he thinks and makes jokes that can offend, but he always makes fun of himself too.
And I, at least, can say one thing very clearly: never once did I feel that any of his remarks were meant as an attack, as belittling or as humiliating. It was always situational comedy. If Jensen hadn't been CEO of NVIDIA, he would have made an outstanding stand-up comedian, always ready with a quip. But as we all know, that's a matter of taste, and saying that I always found it amusing won't calm anyone down.
So here are two stories that show Jensen really has a good heart, and that the campaign against him distorts his image.
This is my personal experience:
NVIDIA gave me the opportunity to do a 30-minute interview with Jensen in Stockholm.
As you can imagine, I was incredibly nervous. Honestly, I was even scared. Me, a small "content creator," getting to meet Jensen in person and talk to him. He makes time even for little people like me. I met him and his staff at a café in Stockholm. We went inside and, as was bound to happen, my camera gear fell out of my backpack onto the floor. My stress level: through the roof. But Jensen stayed calm and relaxed, told me everything was fine and that I didn't need to stress, and put his hand on my shoulder. Not one snide word, no making fun of me. Quite the opposite. He knew I was genuinely stressed and helped me relax.
Then we started the interview. And while we were talking, people kept coming into the café where we were recording. It was a café open to the public. And as you'd expect, the same thing happened again and again: while Jensen and I were talking, guests recognized him and more or less burst into our interview. And Jensen took time for every single one of them. Not one bad word, no irritation, no stupid remark. He gave every guest his time, took photos, had conversations. In the middle of the interview. I was surprised and genuinely moved. No arrogance on his part, just friendly humanity. And that's how an interview scheduled for 30 minutes turned into 60. Simply because Jensen and I had such a good conversation and he kindly gave all those guests extra time on top.
But the most impressive part actually came afterwards. We had been eating a Swedish pastry, it's called “fika” (at least that’s how we called it). And Jensen loved it. After we wrapped up the interview, Jensen went to the trunk of his car, grabbed some cash, went back into the café and bought “fika” for everyone. For himself, his security, his staff, for everyone.
No camera recorded it. Nothing done purely for PR. Nothing meant to make him "look better." Just a human gesture, because he liked the pastry and wanted everyone to enjoy it too. If I hadn't told this story today, it would never have been told. And to me it shows that Jensen is a genuinely good person.
I gain nothing from writing this. Jensen is no longer CEO. And nobody suggested I write this story down.

Google continues to work on a new "Inbox mode" for Antigravity, where users will be able to see threads that require their attention.
It follows a broader shift we see across other Google AI tools, like Gemini (in the works) and Loop (waitlist). This change positions users in the decision-making seat to approve and review AI outcomes, rather than steering them precisely, as a main interface.
Antigravity is also getting new logic to create AI agents from the prompt, distinguished as "For Me" and "For my Team".
It is getting even more interesting now 👀

items.title:
Google recently announced Loop, its new self-improving AI agent that can autonomously work toward a given goal.
Loop is internally called Jitro; interestingly, that was the exact name for Jules v2.
Here is how it works 👀
1. Users start creating a Workspace by connecting it to a selected Github project and adding basic information.
2. Users can create loops manually or select ones that are already predefined (ex., Harden Application Security)
"Custom Loops" can be created via a prompt or by manually filling in the Loop title, icon, and objective.
> "Loops are mid- to long-term objectives for Stitch Loop to continuously work toward. They can range from highly specific to broad, but should always be something code can achieve," says the description.
3. Users can connect additional context in the form of Integrations, Files, Links, or additional repositories.
More than 100 integrations are available there, including services like Jira, Linear, Datadog, Sentry, Notion, Snowflake, Salesforce, Intercom, Discord, Slack, Figma, and many others.
Custom MCPs are supported as well.
4. After creating a workspace, Loop will start digging into your project details and generate its own Skills about the product and product metrics.
These Skills will live in a separate tab and can be edited in the UI in Markdown.
5. When the Workspace is ready, Loop will suggest metrics and goals based on its own research. Users can convert these suggestions into loops right away.
When a Loop is created, it appears as a running process in the main UI.
6. When a Loop is finished, users will see a list of suggestions for every loop, along with a number associated with a target metric and progress status.
Example Loop:
- Goal - Scale Telegram community contributions.
- KPIs - community members, registered contributors, active members.
A high-level goal would be broken down into sub-KPIs. When users open a dedicated Loop page, all these KPIs will be visible on the dashboard.
Below, Users will see a list of Tasks, Skills, and Activity tabs.
Example Task:
- Telegram channel lacks discussion threads and a dedicated bot.
Each task has a detailed description, labels, and the date when it was updated. Below, users will see tabs for Solutions, Activity, and Evidence.
Activity appears as a summary describing what happened, what was done, and the general Timeline.
Evidence contains links to where Loop pulled the context behind this Task. In my example case, it refers to the TestingCatalog website and the Telegram channel from which it pulled all the numbers.
Example Solution:
- Dedicated Telegram Bot API intake bot with editorial triage webhook (implementation task).
This task is an implementation task that has a clear description, Impact, scope, and Risk labeled.
Users can start the task right from this page to begin solution development via Gemini.
When the task is done, users can review its progress and status and monitor its impact on production by pulling updated metrics and KPIs after the release.
What does all this mean? 🤯
Loop follows how "Product work" is done at Google, a model many other companies also use.
Every Workspace in Loop is equivalent to a scope that is normally handled by a complete product engineering team.
It is no longer a place where users play the role of engineering lead and product lead, orchestrating AI agents.
It is a place where the user plays the role of a senior manager managing several engineering teams, which is a big shift on its own.
We are slowly moving towards autonomous AI organizations. One management layer at a time.
I expect it will still take until 2027 for labs to develop the products and models needed to make substantial progress in this area (assuming AI continues to advance in a semi-regulated format as it is now).
Monitoring 🍿

@arcfront は、病院から銀行に至るまで 300 社以上の大企業と提携して、専門家がどのように重要な意思決定を行っているかを記録しています。例には、ソフトウェアのロールバック手順、チップ設計計画、M&A 評価などがあります。
アンシュマン・シン (@anshuman_ssh)
本日、私たちは @Naman_Bhalla と @asxna からの強力なサポートとともに @arcfront を立ち上げます。
1 年も経たないうちに、フロンティア ラボ 5 社のうち 4 社が顧客になりました。
2025 年、AI が ICPC 世界決勝戦で 12 の問題すべてを解決しました。最も優れた人間チームが 11 を解決しました。私はそれらの決勝戦のうち 2 回に出場したので、それがどれほど大きな偉業であるかを知っています。
それでも、同じ AI を財務マネージャーとして社内に導入したり、その他のほぼすべての仕事に導入したりすると、初日から失敗します。
